question: Can exact Fenchel-Young softmax-family losses and scalable softmax approximations be compared in one principled framework that connects classification/ranking consistency, gradient dynamics, estimator bias and variance, computational cost, and recommendation performance?

key_findings.claim: The paper's genuine synthesis is a common comparison grid spanning exact Fenchel-Young losses and approximate partition-function methods; it does not newly derive most individual losses or approximation mechanisms.
key_findings.evidence: Tables 1-4 organize Softmax, Sparsemax, alpha-Entmax, Rankmax, sampled softmax (SSM), NCE, hierarchical softmax (HSM), and a Taylor/RG surrogate by consistency, order preservation, Jacobian behavior, asymptotic/curvature bias, variance, and per-epoch head cost. The underlying F-Y framework, Sparsemax, Entmax, Rankmax, importance-sampled softmax, NCE, HSM, and RG are all attributed to prior papers; the contribution is the cross-family analysis and recommendation study.

key_findings.claim: Under the paper's pointwise multiclass assumptions, the exact Softmax, Sparsemax, and alpha-Entmax losses are argued to be Top-k calibrated and DCG-consistent, with Softmax strictly order preserving and sparse maps only weakly order preserving.
key_findings.evidence: The F-Y/Bregman argument makes the Bayes-optimal probability equal the class posterior. Proposition 3.2 gives Softmax classification, Top-k, and DCG consistency; Proposition 3.3 extends Top-k/DCG consistency to Sparsemax and alpha-Entmax. Proposition 3.5 shows sparse thresholding can map distinct below-threshold logits to equal zero probability, while Theorem 3.6 claims weak order preservation suffices for those metrics.

key_findings.claim: The sparse-map tie argument identifies zero gradients and rank-deficient local geometry, but it overstates the ranking consequence unless inference actually ranks the tied mapped probabilities rather than the original distinct logits.
key_findings.evidence: Sparsemax and Entmax can set p_i=p_j=0 despite s_i>s_j, and Appendix B.2 derives an expected-DCG reduction under uniformly random tie breaking plus gradient bias from inactive classes. Recommender inference normally sorts score logits s, for which those two classes remain ordered. Thus the vanishing-gradient mechanism is real, whereas an inevitable evaluation-time DCG tie requires an additional scoring/tie-breaking assumption not established for the experiments.

anchors.section: Appendix B.2.1 / Expected DCG under ties

key_findings.claim: Rankmax is empirically strong because it concentrates support on the target and hard negatives, but its label-conditioned projection is not a standard label-independent prediction map and therefore does not fit the common Fenchel-Young interpretation as cleanly as the paper implies.
key_findings.evidence: Rankmax chooses an adaptive support containing the ground-truth class and negatives with scores near or above its score, giving sparse gradients focused on difficult comparisons. Appendix B.3 proves weak order preservation for this construction. Because the support and mapping depend explicitly on y during training, there is no single inference-time map p-hat(s) independent of the unknown label analogous to Softmax/Sparsemax/Entmax; the consistency comparison requires care about whether Rankmax is treated as a loss, a training projection, or a prediction rule.

key_findings.claim: The logit-level Jacobian bounds are useful local smoothness facts, but they do not justify the paper's claimed parameter-level linear-convergence ordering for deep recommendation models.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B.4 bounds the Softmax Jacobian spectral norm by 1/2, Sparsemax by 1, alpha-Entmax by at most 1, and gives a support-dependent Rankmax bound. Equation 56 omits the nonlinear-logit Hessian term sum_i (p_i-y_i) nabla_theta^2 s_i from the chain rule. Equation 57 then asserts that adding gamma||theta||^2/2 ensures mu>=gamma strong convexity, which is false for a nonconvex network unless gamma exceeds a global negative-curvature bound that is neither assumed nor proved. SASRec and LightGCN are not strongly convex objectives, so the contraction factor and strict architecture-independent rate ordering do not apply to those experiments.

key_findings.claim: Worst-case Jacobian upper bounds cannot establish that Softmax always optimizes faster than Entmax or Sparsemax, even at the logit level.
key_findings.evidence: The claimed ordering compares sup_s ||J(s)||, not the realized Hessian spectrum, lower curvature, condition number, optimizer trajectory, or time to a common loss. Softmax curvature approaches zero under saturated probabilities, sparse losses are piecewise linear/projective, and the upper bounds need not be attained on the same data. The main text itself concedes approximate objectives with small Jacobian norms need not converge faster because bias matters; the same caution is needed for exact objectives and nonlinear parameterizations.

key_findings.claim: The delta-method table characterizes a conditional log-partition estimator approximation, not a guarantee about the bias, variance, or convergence of a trained recommendation model.
key_findings.evidence: Table 3 and Appendix B.5 expand a random approximation to log Z(s) at fixed logits, yielding for corrected SSM zero asymptotic bias, curvature bias -chi^2(P_s||Q)/(2k), and variance chi^2(P_s||Q)/k; NCE receives a weighted Jensen-Shannon asymptotic term and chi-square variance; HSM and RG receive KL and local Taylor terms. The expansion is asymptotic and conditional on proposal support and finite moments. Experiments report only downstream ranking metrics and do not estimate any divergence, estimator bias, variance, or approximation remainder, so their claimed empirical verification is indirect.

key_findings.claim: The paper directly contradicts itself about corrected sampled Softmax being unbiased at finite sample size.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A.5 says subtracting log q from sampled logits makes the gradient an unbiased estimator of the full Softmax gradient in expectation. Yet Table 3 and Appendix B.5 derive a nonzero O(1/k) curvature bias for the corrected normalized ratio/log estimator. This is the standard self-normalized importance-sampling issue: proposal correction can give consistent/asymptotically unbiased estimation, but the nonlinear finite-k log-normalizer and gradient are generally biased.

key_findings.claim: The narrative that NCE has an irreducible bias and negligible dependence on k is too categorical and conflicts with both the appendix and the SASRec ablation.
key_findings.evidence: The main comparison assigns NCE a positive weighted-JS asymptotic discrepancy and states increasing negatives has negligible influence. Appendix A.5 also says NCE is asymptotically consistent with MLE, while Appendix B.5.3 discusses convergence toward the MLE stationary point as k grows. In SASRec, increasing k from 10 to 100 changes MovieLens NDCG@20 from 0.0174 to 0.1325 and Electronics from 0.0157 to 0.0175 with a non-monotone path, which is far from negligible.

key_findings.claim: The per-epoch complexity table is a head-level asymptotic inventory, not an end-to-end efficiency comparison.
key_findings.evidence: The paper lists Softmax Theta(NC), Sparsemax Theta(NC log C), Entmax Theta(NC log C+N|P|), Rankmax Theta(NC), SSM/NCE Theta(Nk), and HSM Theta(N log C). These counts omit backbone forward/backward cost, sorting/top-k implementation, memory traffic, tree construction, negative sampling, proposal updates, number of epochs, ALS sweeps, and hardware kernels. HSM also uses a different tree-parameterized output, and RG/ALS lacks a directly comparable generic cost entry.

anchors.section: Appendix A.5 / HSM and RG parameterizations

key_findings.claim: On matrix factorization, Softmax is a strong default but not the best loss in most displayed dataset-metric cells.
key_findings.evidence: Softmax reaches MovieLens NDCG@20/Precision@20/Recall@20 of 0.2661/0.1465/0.2937, Electronics 0.0235/0.0027/0.0496, and Gowalla 0.0953/0.0190/0.1716. Rankmax improves MovieLens to 0.2851/0.1543/0.3005 and Gowalla to 0.1031/0.0206/0.1794; RG reaches Electronics 0.0274/0.0030/0.0563; Sparsemax and Entmax also win selected Gowalla/Electronics cells. The title question therefore has an empirically qualified answer rather than 'Softmax alone.'

key_findings.claim: Sparsemax and Entmax degrade sharply in SASRec, while Rankmax remains competitive or better than Softmax, showing that sparsity alone is not the causal explanation.
key_findings.evidence: SASRec Softmax obtains NDCG@20 of 0.1647 on MovieLens, 0.0355 on Electronics, and 0.0470 on Gowalla. Rankmax obtains 0.1789, 0.0357, and 0.0474, respectively, and also improves MovieLens Precision/Recall to 0.0188/0.3756 from 0.0180/0.3599. Sparsemax and especially Entmax suffer large drops. Since Rankmax is itself sparse, performance depends on which examples remain active and its hard-negative construction, not a universal dense-versus-sparse dichotomy.

key_findings.claim: Corrected sampled Softmax can outperform full Softmax in the paper's LightGCN setting, so approximation error is not monotonically reflected in held-out recommendation quality.
key_findings.evidence: On MovieLens-1M LightGCN, SSM records NDCG@20/Precision@20/Recall@20 of 0.2358/0.1339/0.2523, exceeding full Softmax at 0.2279/0.1316/0.2488. Sparsemax is 0.1695/0.0983/0.1755, while Entmax and Rankmax are near 0.121 NDCG. The result may reflect stochastic regularization, proposal effects, or optimization, and it prevents interpreting smaller estimator bias as a universal ordering of downstream performance.

key_findings.claim: Increasing sampled negatives generally helps SSM, but the magnitude is architecture- and dataset-dependent and is confounded with additional computation.
key_findings.evidence: For MF, increasing k from 10 to 100 raises SSM NDCG@20 from 0.2504 to 0.2644 on MovieLens and 0.0611 to 0.0848 on Gowalla, with only 0.0235 to 0.0246 on Electronics. For SASRec it raises MovieLens from 0.0179 to 0.1524 and Electronics from 0.0148 to 0.0260. No fixed-wall-time or fixed-number-of-logit-evaluations comparison separates estimator quality from extra negatives.

key_findings.claim: Dynamic negative sampling improves both SSM and NCE, but the experiment does not directly verify the proposed divergence-alignment mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: For MF NCE, switching from uniform sampling to DNS increases NDCG@20 from 0.2423 to 0.2769 on MovieLens, 0.0238 to 0.0273 on Electronics, and 0.0514 to 0.0599 on Gowalla; SSM also improves. DNS selects the top 100 candidates from a pool of 500 and therefore changes hardness and compute. The paper does not estimate Q, P_s, chi-square divergence, bias, variance, false-negative rate, or proposal-update cost, so reduced divergence is plausible but not measured.

key_findings.claim: The empirical evidence has no reported uncertainty despite explicit claims that differences are significant.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix C says standard deviations are omitted because performance differences are 'already highly significant,' but the paper does not state the number of random seeds, provide dispersion, confidence intervals, paired tests, p-values, or a multiple-comparison protocol. Many differences are in the fourth decimal place and hyperparameters are selected from a learning-rate grid, so significance and ranking stability cannot be independently assessed.

anchors.section: Appendix C.1.1 / Datasets and evaluation protocol

key_findings.claim: The experiment tests implicit recommendation catalogs of at most 63,001 items, not the broad classification, language-modeling, or truly extreme-class regimes emphasized in the motivation.
key_findings.evidence: The three datasets are MovieLens-1M (6,038 users, 3,307 items, 835,789 retained interactions), Amazon Electronics (192,403 users, 63,001 items, 1,689,188 interactions), and Gowalla (29,858 users, 40,981 items, 1,027,370 interactions), with MF and SASRec across all, and LightGCN only on MovieLens. HSM and RG are restricted to MF because of output/ALS incompatibility. No image classification, language modeling, retrieval at millions of classes, calibration, or rare-class test is included.

key_findings.claim: The multiclass consistency proof and the multi-positive recommendation protocol are not fully connected.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A defines the Bayes target as a one-hot multiclass label and obtains posterior matching; a footnote handles multi-label y outside the simplex by normalizing y/||y||_1. Precision, Recall, and NDCG depend on variable-cardinality binary relevance sets and cutoff normalization, while experiments treat user-item interactions and random per-user splits. The paper does not prove that this normalization plus its training-instance construction yields Bayes consistency for the exact multi-positive NDCG@20 protocol.

method.core_idea: Place exact Softmax-family losses and scalable approximations into a common Fenchel-Young risk view, compare their metric consistency and score-map geometry, analyze approximate log-partition errors with a delta method, inventory head complexity, and test whether those theoretical distinctions predict implicit-recommendation performance.
method.mechanism: A convex regularizer Omega on the probability simplex induces a conjugate, prediction map grad Omega*, and Fenchel-Young loss with residual gradient p-hat-y. Bregman posterior matching plus order preservation connects exact losses to Top-k/DCG consistency; sparse maps are classified as weakly rather than strictly order preserving. Jacobian spectral norms are used as curvature proxies. Random approximations are represented through a nuisance variable xi and expanded around their expected partition estimator to separate asymptotic discrepancy, second-order curvature bias, and variance. Complexity is counted per output head, then Softmax, Sparsemax, Entmax, Rankmax, SSM, NCE, HSM, and RG are compared with MF, SASRec, and one LightGCN setting.
assumptions: Pointwise multiclass posterior matching and order preservation transfer to the paper's multi-positive, cutoff-NDCG recommendation construction.
Ties in sparse predicted probabilities determine evaluation ordering even when inference can rank the underlying distinct logits.
Rankmax's ground-truth-conditioned support can be treated within the same label-independent prediction-map framework as standard F-Y losses.
The score map is sufficiently regular and proposal Q has support wherever P_s does, with finite moments and small enough delta-method remainder.
Asymptotic fixed-logit partition-estimator bias and variance predict end-to-end trained-model quality.
Equation 56's Gauss-Newton-like term is the full parameter Hessian; this implicitly requires logits linear in parameters or a vanishing residual second-derivative term.
L2 regularization makes the deep objectives globally strongly convex; this is not true without an explicit negative-curvature bound.
Worst-case Jacobian upper bounds track realized condition numbers and optimization speed under Adam across different losses.
The HSM tree output and flat-score losses are comparable despite different parameters, representation capacity, and backbone compatibility.
The RG Taylor approximation is accurate near the origin and model logits stay in that local regime.
Per-head asymptotic cost represents end-to-end wall time across MF, SASRec, and LightGCN implementations.
Random per-user train/validation/test splitting provides an unbiased evaluation for sequential recommendation and does not leak future interactions.
The unreported number of runs and omitted standard deviations are sufficient for claims of significance.
Datasets with at most 63,001 items represent conclusions about exceedingly large class spaces.

techniques.role: Derives a prediction map and convex surrogate jointly from a simplex regularizer.
Connects population-risk minimization to the true class posterior under regularity assumptions.
Separates dense Softmax ordering from sparse threshold-induced probability ties.
Uses score-map Jacobians as local smoothness proxies for exact and approximate losses.
Expands approximate log partition functions into asymptotic, curvature-bias, and variance terms.
Expresses leading SSM bias and variance through chi-square divergence between model and proposal distributions.
Builds a sparse target-conditioned support around the ground-truth score and harder negatives.
Uses proposal-corrected sampled logits to reduce full-catalog normalization cost.
Recasts density learning as data-versus-noise binary classification.
Factorizes class probability along a tree of local softmax decisions.
Approximates the log partition near zero with a quadratic objective compatible with ALS for MF.
Selects hard negatives from a larger candidate pool to alter proposal alignment.
Plots ranking quality against wall time to supplement per-epoch complexity claims.
Visualizes how each loss allocates gradient magnitude across targets and negative scores.

limitations: Author-stated in Appendix D: an unbiased small-k sampled estimator and a theory directly aligned to truncated NDCG@K remain open problems.
Author-stated: HSM uses a different tree-structured output and cannot be plugged naturally into every backbone; RG/ALS is likewise restricted to MF.
Author-stated: societal impact is expected to be limited, while inherited data bias and environmental cost remain possible concerns.
Reviewer-identified: Equation 56 omits second derivatives of nonlinear logits, invalidating the stated general parameter-Hessian bound.
Reviewer-identified: L2 regularization does not automatically make SASRec, LightGCN, or nonlinear MF objectives globally strongly convex; the linear-convergence theorem is inapplicable as stated.
Reviewer-identified: worst-case Jacobian upper bounds are not realized condition numbers and do not prove a universal Softmax>Entmax>Sparsemax optimization ordering.
Reviewer-identified: corrected sampled Softmax is described as finite-sample gradient-unbiased in Appendix A.5 despite the paper's own O(1/k) curvature-bias derivation.
Reviewer-identified: the NCE bias/k narrative is internally inconsistent with both its stated MLE asymptotics and the large SASRec k effect.
Reviewer-identified: delta-method expressions are local/asymptotic fixed-logit approximations; remainders and required proposal/moment conditions are not empirically checked.
Reviewer-identified: no experiment measures the chi-square, JS, or KL quantities that supposedly explain downstream behavior.
Reviewer-identified: the consistency proof is pointwise multiclass and does not rigorously bridge to variable-cardinality, multi-positive NDCG@20 under the exact experimental sampling protocol.
Reviewer-identified: Rankmax's label-dependent support complicates treating it as a common label-independent F-Y prediction map.
Reviewer-identified: sparse probability ties do not necessarily induce ranking ties when inference sorts original logits, so the DCG-tie mechanism is protocol-dependent.
Reviewer-identified: RG's O(||s||^3) error is local around zero, but logit norms and approximation remainder are never reported.
Reviewer-identified: HSM is a different output parameterization, so its KL discrepancy and accuracy are not a controlled drop-in loss comparison.
Reviewer-identified: per-epoch complexity excludes backbone and systems costs and is not validated with numeric runtime/memory tables.
Reviewer-identified: standard deviations are deliberately omitted without reporting seeds or any actual significance test.
Reviewer-identified: model selection over learning rates and three metrics is insufficiently specified and may permit metric-wise best checkpoints or multiple-comparison optimism.
Reviewer-identified: random per-user splits can leak future information into SASRec and do not test temporal generalization.
Reviewer-identified: only three recommendation datasets are studied, the largest catalog has 63,001 items, LightGCN is tested only on MovieLens, and HSM/RG only with MF.
Reviewer-identified: no classification, language modeling, calibrated probability, rare-class, or million-class benchmark supports the paper's cross-domain motivation.
Reviewer-identified: DNS changes sampling hardness and computation simultaneously and can increase false negatives; neither factor is audited.
Reviewer-identified: the paper has no dedicated limitations section in the main text despite several theorem-to-experiment scope gaps.
failure_modes: Sparsemax or Entmax can push many classes off support, eliminate their gradients, and create large flat regions before a hard negative is recovered.
Dense Softmax can continue spending gradient on easy negatives after the relevant ordering is already correct.
Rankmax can depend sensitively on target-conditioned support construction and is not available as the same probability map when y is unknown.
Corrected SSM remains finite-k biased because it normalizes a random importance-sampling ratio; rare high-weight negatives can inflate variance.
A proposal Q with poor support or large mismatch from P_s can make chi-square bias/variance terms huge or undefined.
NCE can optimize a data-versus-noise discrimination problem whose finite-k optimum and conditioning differ from full Softmax MLE.
HSM can encode a poor tree, lengthen paths for important labels, and change output capacity rather than merely approximate a fixed flat head.
RG/Taylor loss can deviate substantially when logits leave the small-norm neighborhood around its expansion point.
DNS can mine false negatives, add a costly candidate-ranking stage, and improve metrics through hardness rather than the claimed proposal-divergence reduction.
A loss can have a smaller fixed-logit estimator error yet a worse trained model because stochasticity, regularization, backbone interaction, and optimization path differ.
SASRec can exploit random-split future interactions, overstating sequential recommendation generalization.
Metric-wise checkpoint or hyperparameter selection can exaggerate small fourth-decimal differences when uncertainty is omitted.
Worst-case smoothness analysis can predict fast optimization while saturated Softmax produces nearly zero curvature and slow practical progress.
Adding ordinary L2 regularization to a deep network can leave negative-curvature directions, so strong-convexity step-size and contraction guarantees fail.
Head-only complexity can select an approximation that is asymptotically attractive but slower end to end due to sorting, sampling, memory, or backbone dominance.
reusable_insights: Separate population metric consistency, score-map geometry, finite-sample estimator error, optimization trajectory, and systems cost; none alone orders trained-model quality.
For any sampled log-normalizer, distinguish unbiased estimation of an unnormalized sum from bias introduced by a logarithm or self-normalized ratio.
When moving a logit-level Hessian result to model parameters, include both the Gauss-Newton term and residual-weighted second derivatives of the logits.
Do not infer global strong convexity of a neural objective merely by adding L2 regularization; quantify negative curvature or state a linear-model restriction.
Report realized Hessian/gradient statistics and time-to-quality rather than ranking methods by worst-case Jacobian upper bounds.
Audit whether a purported prediction map depends on the training label; label-conditioned projections require a separate inference definition.
For sparse losses, report active-set churn, recovery of off-support hard negatives, and whether evaluation ranks probabilities or pre-projection logits.
Validate delta-method explanations by measuring proposal divergence, estimator bias/variance, and remainder behavior at logits encountered during training.
Compare negative-sampling methods at fixed wall time, scored-candidate count, and false-negative rate in addition to fixed k.
State whether multi-label targets are normalized and prove consistency for the exact cutoff metric and data construction being evaluated.
Use chronological splits for sequential recommendation and report repeated-run uncertainty before interpreting small differences.
Treat HSM/tree outputs and ALS-specific surrogates as system designs rather than drop-in losses unless parameterization and compute are controlled.
open_questions: Can the convergence analysis be repaired for linear logits and then extended to nonconvex networks with a valid stationarity or local-PL guarantee?
What are the exact finite-k bias and variance of the SSM gradient, not only the conditional log-partition estimator, under adaptive proposals?
Can one reconcile the weighted-JS NCE term with classical NCE consistency and empirically map its dependence on k?
Does the weak-order-preservation theorem imply consistency for the exact multi-positive NDCG@20 protocol, including target normalization and tie handling?
How should Rankmax be defined at inference without a ground-truth label, and which prediction object is used for calibration claims?
Do probability-space ties actually change recommendation rankings when the implementation sorts logits, and how often do relevant items fall off support?
How accurate is the RG quadratic approximation over the observed logit-norm distribution, and can expansion centers be adapted during training?
Do the conclusions reproduce on million-class language modeling, extreme classification, large-scale retrieval, and calibrated multiclass prediction?
How do all losses compare under chronological splits, repeated seeds, paired tests, and fixed end-to-end wall time/memory?
Can measured chi-square/JS/KL divergence predict when DNS, SSM, NCE, or HSM beats exact Softmax?
What fraction of DNS candidates are false negatives, and is its gain retained when mining compute is charged to the budget?
Can a small-k estimator be unbiased under restricted structural assumptions, or can lower-bound results formally rule it out in this setting?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning with Fenchel-Young Losses
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational direct prior for the paper's exact-loss unification, Bregman interpretation, convexity, calibration, sparse regularizers, and residual gradients.
competitive_landscape.difference: It already develops the broad Fenchel-Young framework across classification, ranking, and structured prediction. The reviewed paper specializes and juxtaposes several F-Y losses with approximate Softmax heads, adds Jacobian/delta/complexity tables, and evaluates recommendation; the core F-Y unification itself is not new.

competitive_landscape.title: From Softmax to Sparsemax: A Sparse Model of Attention and Multi-Label Classification
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct source of Sparsemax, its simplex projection, sparse Jacobian, and sparse analogue of logistic loss.
competitive_landscape.difference: It already derives Sparsemax properties and efficient backpropagation with multi-label and attention experiments. The reviewed paper contributes a comparative WOP/consistency and recommendation narrative, but its zero-gradient and support geometry are inherited mechanisms.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Sequence-to-Sequence Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct source of alpha-Entmax and scalable sparse transformations between Softmax and Sparsemax.
competitive_landscape.difference: It already introduces controllable sparse output/attention maps, gradients, and large-vocabulary algorithms with NLP evaluations. The reviewed paper adds cross-loss consistency/optimization comparisons in recommendation, not the Entmax family itself.

competitive_landscape.title: Rankmax: An Adaptive Projection Alternative to the Softmax Function
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct source of the target-conditioned adaptive sparse projection that is the strongest exact-loss competitor in several reviewed experiments.
competitive_landscape.difference: Rankmax already contributes adaptive support, efficient implementation, and empirical gains over non-adaptive projections. The reviewed paper adds a WOP/hard-negative interpretation and recommendation comparison, while leaving the label-dependent inference-map issue unresolved.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Effectiveness of Sampled Softmax Loss for Item Recommendation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct recommendation-specific predecessor analyzing sampled Softmax, ranking alignment, popularity, hard negatives, and backbone interaction.
competitive_landscape.difference: It already asks whether SSM suits recommendation and reports theory plus four-dataset experiments. The reviewed paper broadens comparison to exact sparse losses, NCE/HSM/RG, and a delta-method table, but does not originate SSM-for-recommendation or its hard-negative motivation.

competitive_landscape.title: PSL: Rethinking and Improving Softmax Loss from Pairwise Perspective for Recommendation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct Softmax-loss theory and ranking-surrogate competitor in recommendation, focused on DCG alignment and false negatives.
competitive_landscape.difference: PSL already critiques standard Softmax's ranking alignment and replaces its exponential pairwise activation, with NeurIPS 2024 recommendation experiments. The reviewed work instead compares a wider catalog through F-Y consistency and approximation error, but does not test PSL head to head.

competitive_landscape.title: Correcting the LogQ Correction: Revisiting Sampled Softmax for Large-Scale Retrieval
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct current competitor on finite-sample bias in proposal-corrected sampled Softmax for large-scale recommendation retrieval.
competitive_landscape.difference: It shows the common logQ derivation mishandles the always-present positive and proposes a refined correction, directly narrowing any claim that ordinary corrected SSM is unbiased. The reviewed paper gives a broader delta-method taxonomy but does not implement or compare this refined correction.

competitive_landscape.title: Strategies for Training Large Vocabulary Neural Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct prior systematic comparison of full Softmax, HSM, target sampling, NCE, and self-normalization under large vocabularies.
competitive_landscape.difference: It already compares speed/accuracy trade-offs, rare-word behavior, and alternative approximations across three language-model benchmarks. The reviewed paper contributes a unified theoretical table and recommendation study, but its empirical scope is narrower in task domain and catalog scale.

competitive_landscape.title: On Using Very Large Target Vocabulary for Neural Machine Translation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Primary importance-sampled Softmax predecessor for avoiding full-vocabulary normalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: It already uses proposal sampling to make very large target vocabularies tractable and evaluates translation quality. The reviewed paper abstracts such estimators through delta-method bias/variance and transfers them to recommendation, without a language-model or translation replication.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a principled foundation for choosing among the complete Softmax family by jointly establishing exact-loss classification/ranking consistency, Jacobian-based convergence behavior, a systematic bias-variance decomposition for approximations with convergence guarantees, per-epoch complexity, and aligned recommendation evidence.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper presents a compact cross-family taxonomy, WOP/SOP results, score-map Jacobian bounds, fixed-logit delta expansions for SSM/NCE/HSM/RG, asymptotic cost counts, and MF/SASRec/LightGCN experiments with negative-count and proposal ablations. Searches across (1) Fenchel-Young/Bregman loss unification, (2) Sparsemax/Entmax/Rankmax projection losses, (3) sampled Softmax/NCE/HSM large-vocabulary approximation, (4) recommendation-specific sampled Softmax and pairwise Softmax losses, and (5) finite-sample logQ correction/bias found no earlier primary paper with this exact all-in-one table-plus-recommendation package, but every component family and several closer domain-specific analyses predate it.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The broad comparative packaging and attempt to put exact and approximate heads on one page appear novel. The strongest claimed theoretical novelty is substantially weaker than advertised: the parameter-level convergence guarantee drops a Hessian term and assumes false global strong convexity; the delta analysis is a conditional asymptotic log-partition calculation rather than trained-model convergence; and finite-k SSM unbiasedness is internally contradicted. Prior F-Y, sparse projection, large-vocabulary, SSM-recommendation, PSL, and corrected-logQ work already contains the main ingredients. The durable contribution is therefore a useful taxonomy and a broad recommender benchmark with revealing negative results, not a complete principled ordering or general convergence foundation.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text review completed end to end on all 34 indexed pages: main paper, equations, Tables 1-4 and related work (pp. 1-11); Appendices A.1-A.5 covering metrics, F-Y/Bregman/mirror-descent foundations and every approximation (pp. 12-15); Appendix B proofs, sparse-tie analysis, Rankmax, convergence derivations, and delta method (pp. 15-24); Appendix C datasets, implementation details, every numeric result table and dynamics/gradient figure (pp. 25-32 and p. 34); and Appendix D Top-K discussion (pp. 32-34). Rendered equations and tables were inspected where extraction was ambiguous, especially Eq. 56's parameter Hessian, Eq. 57's strong-convexity assertion, Table 3's SSM/NCE terms, and Tables 6-12. Author reports, reviewer inferences, and contradiction audits are labeled separately. Competitor discovery used five query families: 'Fenchel-Young losses Bregman classification ranking', 'Sparsemax Entmax Rankmax sparse projection', 'sampled softmax NCE hierarchical softmax large vocabulary', 'sampled softmax recommendation pairwise softmax ranking', and 'sampled softmax logQ finite-sample bias correction'. Nine direct primary arXiv/proceedings records were opened and current versions pinned on 2026-08-23. No earlier record was found with the exact full cross-family synthesis, but all loss families and multiple recommendation/large-vocabulary comparisons are prior. Confidence is high for provenance, reported values, and the identified Eq. 56/57 defects; confidence is lower for reconstructing authors' intended scope where main-text rhetoric exceeds the formal assumptions.
